<div class="diatribe-meta">Book III · 4 paragraphs · <span class="canonical" title="Canonical reference">III 10</span></div>

<nav class="chapter-nav"><a href="3-09.html">Previous discourse</a><a class="chapter-home" href="../index.html">Home</a><a href="3-11.html">Next discourse</a></nav>

<div class="paragraph-list">
<p>WHEN the need of each opinion comes, we ought to have it in readiness:<a class="note-ref" id="noteref-1" href="#note-1" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 1"><sup>1</sup></a> on the occasion of breakfast, such opinions as relate to breakfast; in the bath, those that concern the bath; in bed, those that concern bed.</p>
<span class="lg"> <span class="l">Let sleep not come upon thy languid eyes</span> <span class="l">Before each daily action thou hast scann’d;</span> <span class="l">What’s done amiss, what done, what left undone;</span> <span class="l">From first to last examine all, and then</span> <span class="l">Blame what is wrong, in what is right rejoice.</span> </span>
<p>And we ought to retain these verses in such way that we may use them, not that we may utter them aloud, as when we exclaim <q>Paean Apollo.</q><a class="note-ref" id="noteref-3" href="#note-3" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 3"><sup>3</sup></a> Again in fever we should have ready such opinions as concern a fever; and we ought not, as soon as the fever begins, to lose and forget all. (A man who has a fever) may say: If I philosophize any longer, may I be hanged: wherever I go, I must take care of the poor body, that a fever may not come.<a class="note-ref" id="noteref-4" href="#note-4" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 4"><sup>4</sup></a> But what is philosophizing? Is it not a preparation against events which may happen? Do you not understand that you are saying something of this kind? <q>If I shall still prepare myself to bear with patience what happens, may I be hanged.</q> But this is just as if a man after receiving blows should give up the Pancratium. In the Pancratium it is in our power to desist and not to receive blows. But in the other matter if we give up philosophy, what shall we gain? What then should a man say on the occasion of each painful thing? It was for this that I exercised myself, for this I disciplined myself. God says to you, Give me a proof that you have duly practised athletics,<a class="note-ref" id="noteref-5" href="#note-5" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 5"><sup>5</sup></a> that you have eaten what you ought, that you have been exercised, that you have obeyed the aliptes (the oiler and rubber). Then do you show yourself weak when the time for action comes? Now is the time for the fever. Let it be borne well. Now is the time for thirst, bear it well; now is the time for hunger, bear it well. Is it not in your power? who shall hinder you? The physician will hinder you from drinking; but he cannot prevent you from bearing thirst well: and he will hinder you from eating; but he cannot prevent you from bearing hunger well.</p>
<p>But I cannot attend to my philosophical studies.<a class="note-ref" id="noteref-6" href="#note-6" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 6"><sup>6</sup></a> And for what purpose do you follow them? Slave, is it not that you may be happy, that you may be constant, is it not that you may be in a state conformable to nature and live so? What hinders you when you have a fever from having your ruling faculty conformable to nature? Here is the proof of the thing, here is the test of the philosopher. For this also is a part of life, like walking, like sailing, like journeying by land, so also is fever. Do you read when you are walking? No. Nor do you when you have a fever. But if you walk about well, you have all that belongs to a man who walks. If you bear a fever well, you have all that belongs to a man in a fever. What is it to bear a fever well? Not to blame God or man; not to be afflicted at that which happens, to expect death well and nobly, to do what must be done: when the physician comes in, not to be frightened at what he says; nor if he says, <q>you are doing well,</q><a class="note-ref" id="noteref-7" href="#note-7" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 7"><sup>7</sup></a> to be overjoyed. For what good has he told you? and when you were in health, what good was that to you? And even if he says, <q>you are in a bad way,</q> do not despond. For what is it to be ill? is it that you are near the severance of the soul and the body? what harm is there in this? If you are not near now, will you not afterwards be near? Is the world going to be turned upside down when you are dead? Why then do you flatter the physician?<a class="note-ref" id="noteref-8" href="#note-8" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 8"><sup>8</sup></a> Why do you say if you please, master, I shall be well?<a class="note-ref" id="noteref-9" href="#note-9" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 9"><sup>9</sup></a> Why do you give him an opportunity of raising his eyebrows (being proud; or showing his importance)?<a class="note-ref" id="noteref-10" href="#note-10" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 10"><sup>10</sup></a> Do you not value a physician, as you do a shoemaker when he is measuring your foot, or a carpenter when he is building your house, and so treat the physician as to the body which is not yours, but by nature dead? He who has a fever has an opportunity of doing this: if he does these things, he has what belongs to him. For it is not the business of a philosopher to look after these externals, neither his wine nor his oil nor his poor body, but his own ruling power. But as to externals how must he act? so far as not to be careless about them. Where then is there reason for fear? where is there then still reason for anger, and of fear about what belongs to others, about things which are of no value? For we ought to have these two principles in readiness, that except the will nothing is good nor bad; and that we ought not to lead events, but to follow them.<a class="note-ref" id="noteref-11" href="#note-11" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 11"><sup>11</sup></a>—My brother<a class="note-ref" id="noteref-12" href="#note-12" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="note 12"><sup>12</sup></a> ought not to have behaved thus to me.—No; but he will see to that: and, however he may behave, I will conduct myself towards him as I ought. For this is my own business: that belongs to another; no man can prevent this, the other thing can be hindered.</p>
</div>

<section class="notes">
<h2>Notes</h2>
<ol class="note-list">
<li class="note" id="note-1" role="doc-endnote"><p>M. Antoninus, iii. 13. <q>As physicians have always their instruments and knives ready for cases which suddenly require their skill, so do thou have principles (<span class="foreign" lang="grc">δόγματα</span>) ready for the understanding of things divine and human, and for doing every thing, even the smallest, with a recollection of the bond which unites the divine and human to one another. For neither wilt thou do anything well which pertains to man without at the same time having a reference to things divine; nor the contrary.</q></p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-1" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-2" role="doc-endnote"><p>These verses are from the Golden verses attributed to Pythagoras. See iv. 6. 32.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-2" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-3" role="doc-endnote"><p>The beginning of a form of prayer, as in Macrobius, Sat. i 17: <q lang="lat" class="foreign">namque Vestales Virgines ita indigitant; Apollo Maedice, Apollo Paean.</q></p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-3" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-4" role="doc-endnote"><p>This passage is obscure. See Schweig.’s note here, and also his note on a. 6.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-4" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-5" role="doc-endnote"><p><span class="foreign" lang="grc">εἰ νομίμως ἤθλησας</span>. <q>St. Paul hath made use of this very expression <span class="foreign" lang="grc">ἐὰν μὴ νομίμως ἀθλήσῃ</span>, 2 Tim. ii. 3.</q> Mrs. Carter.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-5" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-6" role="doc-endnote"><p>The Greek is <span class="foreign" lang="grc">οὐ φιλολογῶ</span>. See Schweighaeuser’s note.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-6" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-7" role="doc-endnote"><p>See ii 18, 14.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-7" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-8" role="doc-endnote"><p>Et quid opus Cratero magnos promittere montes? Persius, iii. 65. Craterus was a physician.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-8" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-9" role="doc-endnote"><p>Upton compares Matthew, viii. 2. <q>Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.</q></p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-9" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-10" role="doc-endnote"><p>Compare M. Antoninus, iv. 48. <span class="foreign" lang="grc">τᾶς ὀφρῦς ... συσπάσαντες</span>.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-10" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-11" role="doc-endnote"><p>To this Stoic precept Horace (<cite>Epist. i. 1. 19</cite>) opposes that of Aristippus. <span class="verse-quote" lang="lat" class="foreign"> <span class="l">Et mihi res, non me rebus, subjungere conor.</span> </span> Both wisely said, if they are rightly taken. Schweig., who refers to i. 12. 17.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-11" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-12" role="doc-endnote"><p>Lord Shaftesbury proposed to read <span class="foreign" lang="grc">τὸν ἰατρόν</span> for <span class="foreign" lang="grc">τὸν ἀδελφόν</span>. But see Schweig.’s note.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-12" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
</ol>
</section>
